title: LLM Position Bias: Does Naming an Option First Change an AI's Answer?
author: ritzaco
snippet: Since the beginning of time, LLMs have always just agreed with their users. In a comparison where an LLM didn't know what to agree with, it would just choose the first-named option, assuming it was the first one that came to the user's mind for a reason. The reason is far less…
excerpt: Since the beginning of time, LLMs have always just agreed with their users. In a comparison where an LLM didn't know what to agree with, it would just choose the first-named option, assuming it was the first one that came to the user's mind for a reason. The reason is far less complex than that. Researchers call it position bias, and we wanted to know how much of it today's AI agents still have. We asked Claude Code to choose between 100 pairs of options, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, Slack or Microsoft Teams, McDonald's or Burger King, and heads or tails, 10 times with each option named first. In 72 of the 100 pairs, the agent gave the same answer in all 20 runs, whatever the order. But when it had no real favourite, the order decided the answer. On a coin toss, it called whichever side we named first 19 times out of 20. (Yes, that means you can rig the coin toss when Claude picks who pays for lunch. No, you shouldn't.) This article covers which pairs the order moved, the statistics behind the result, and how to check whether the order is deciding an answer you get from an agent. How we tested All 2,000 sessions used Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) in Claude Code 2.1.326, on 25 and 26 November 2026. Each run was a fresh session in an empty folder, under a clean Claude Code profile with no tools, MCP servers, plugins or memory. Every prompt had the same shape: one sentence of context, then "Should I go with A or B? End your answer with one line: PICK: <name>." The two orders used the same context sentence, so the only difference was which name came first. We ran the 2,000 sessions in a shuffled order so time of day couldn't line up with the order of the names, and we fixed the hypotheses and tests below before the first run. The option named first won 1,031 of the 2,000 runs, or 51.6%. If the order made no difference, you'd expect about 50%.
